idiom_name: raise (aliased as fail) at the first violated precondition
implementation_notes: Ruby names the pattern in its core: Kernel#raise is aliased as Kernel#fail, so fail is literally the method to call when an operation cannot continue. A precondition is one line - fail ArgumentError, 'tenant required' unless tenant - and exceptions unwind to the nearest rescue, with ArgumentError/TypeError/KeyError the standard classes for caller mistakes and custom classes for domain refusals; ensure blocks release resources on both paths. The fail-slow counterpart is idiomatic too (rescue and continue, or rescue => e with only a log line), so fail-fast in Ruby is mostly a convention about where raising is allowed, backed by tests rather than a compiler.
code_sketch:
def acquire(pool, tenant)
  fail ArgumentError, 'tenant required' if tenant.to_s.empty?
  session = pool.try_acquire(tenant)
  fail PoolExhausted, tenant unless session   # refuse immediately, do not enqueue
  session
ensure
  pool.metrics&.record_attempt(tenant)        # runs on the abort path too
end
pitfalls: A bare rescue only catches StandardError, and an empty rescue body continues silently; Exception subclasses such as SignalException or NoMemoryError must not be rescued at all if the process should fail fast.
ensure runs during unwinding, so code in it can raise a different exception and replace the original failure - the cleanup must not itself fail fast.
Without checked exceptions or types, the fail-fast contract lives only in tests and documentation: a caller that rescues broadly will keep going where the design intended refusal.
